title: Cardiac Muscle Contraction
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows one heartbeat in a ventricular myocyte: the ion currents of the action potential and its long refractory period, the conversion of that action potential into a rise in cytosolic Ca2+ by calcium-induced calcium release, the removal of Ca2+ that lets the ventricle relax, and the two ways the heart grades its force, sympathetic signaling and stretch. Board questions usually describe a change, such as a blocked channel, altered plasma K+, ischemia, or a larger end-diastolic volume, and ask you to predict its effect. Each prediction rests on knowing which current dominates each phase, where activator Ca2+ comes from and where it goes, which steps consume ATP, and why the heart cannot recruit cells or summate twitches.
prerequisites: Resting membrane potential, equilibrium potentials, and the Nernst equation
Voltage-gated channel states (closed, open, inactivated) and the Na+/K+-ATPase
Skeletal muscle sarcomere structure and the sliding filament mechanism
G protein-coupled receptors, Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A
Histology of cardiac muscle: intercalated discs, T tubules, and sarcoplasmic reticulum

connections.how: The ventricular action potential forms the QRS complex, ST segment, and T wave, and its K+ currents set the QT interval.
Sarcomere length-tension behavior is the cellular basis of the Frank-Starling mechanism, ventricular function curves, and pressure-volume loops.
Contraction and relaxation both consume ATP, so the balance of coronary O2 supply and myocardial demand decides whether the myocyte can keep beating.

connections.to: Ischemic heart disease (CV-18-C) and heart failure (CV-18-B)
connections.how: ATP loss, acidosis, Ca2+ overload, reduced SERCA2a, and desensitized beta-1 signaling explain stiff, weak, and slowly relaxing myocardium.
Contrasting RyR1 mechanical coupling, motor unit recruitment, and calmodulin-based regulation with cardiac mechanisms is a common source of board questions.

terms.def: A tissue whose cells are electrically joined by gap junctions so that excitation of one cell spreads to all of them and they contract as a unit.
A K+ current that conducts well near the resting potential but very little at depolarized potentials, holding the resting myocyte near the K+ equilibrium potential.
The interval after an upstroke during which no stimulus, however strong, can produce a propagated action potential, because too few fast Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation.
The L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channel of the T tubule; Cav1.2 in heart and Cav1.1 in skeletal muscle.
The Ca2+ release channel of the cardiac sarcoplasmic reticulum, opened by a rise in Ca2+ on its cytosolic side.
The process by which a small trigger influx of Ca2+ through L-type channels opens RyR2 and releases a much larger amount of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
The cardiac junction where one T tubule lies against one terminal cisterna of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, placing L-type channels close to clusters of RyR2.
The sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase of cardiac muscle, which uses ATP to pump cytosolic Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
A small sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane protein that inhibits SERCA2a when unphosphorylated and releases that inhibition when phosphorylated.
A sarcolemmal transporter that moves 3 Na+ into the cell for each Ca2+ moved out, using the Na+ gradient as its energy source.
Inotropy is the force and speed of contraction at a given sarcomere length; lusitropy is the rate of relaxation.
The increase in myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity when a cardiac sarcomere is stretched, which makes force rise more steeply with length than filament overlap alone predicts.

sections.title: The ventricular action potential and the refractory period

blocks.text: Gap junctions in the intercalated discs pass current between myocytes, so the ventricle behaves as a functional syncytium and each cell is brought to threshold by a depolarized neighbor.

At rest (phase 4) the membrane sits at about -85 to -90 mV, near EK (about -95 mV with K+ of 140 mmol/L inside and 4 mmol/L outside), because the inward rectifier IK1 dominates resting conductance. Inward rectification is the key property: on depolarization, intracellular Mg2+ and polyamines plug the IK1 pore, so outward K+ current nearly stops. This gives working myocytes a stable resting potential (nodal cells have little IK1, CV-7) and limits K+ loss during the plateau.

At a threshold of about -70 mV, fast Na+ channels (Nav1.5, gene SCN5A) open in a positive feedback loop that drives the membrane to about +20 mV within 1 to 2 ms; this steep upstroke sets conduction velocity. The channels inactivate within milliseconds and stay inactivated until repolarization. Phase 1 is a brief notch from Na+ channel inactivation and transient outward K+ current (Ito). In phase 2, L-type Ca2+ channels (Cav1.2) carry a sustained inward current balanced by small outward K+ currents, holding the membrane near 0 mV for about 0.2 s; this Ca2+ is the trigger for contraction (C02). In phase 3, L-type channels inactivate, the delayed rectifiers IKr (KCNH2, hERG) and IKs (KCNQ1) grow, and below about -40 mV IK1 unblocks and completes repolarization.

blocks.text: Refractory periods and why the heart cannot be tetanized

Because inactivated Na+ channels cannot reset until the membrane repolarizes, no stimulus can produce a propagated action potential from the upstroke through the plateau into phase 3. This effective refractory period lasts about 0.25 to 0.3 s and ends near -50 to -60 mV. In the following relative refractory period (about 0.05 s), only a stronger than normal stimulus fires the cell, and the upstroke is slower and smaller. Unlike skeletal muscle, whose brief refractory period allows twitches to summate into tetanus, cardiac refractoriness lasts nearly as long as contraction, so the ventricle must relax and refill before the next beat. The long refractory period also resists reentry; uneven shortening by ischemia or prolonged repolarization in long QT syndromes undermines this protection. Low plasma K+ reduces IKr and IK1, lengthening phase 3 and favoring afterdepolarizations.

blocks.title: Predicting the effect of hyperkalemia
blocks.text: Plasma K+ rises from 4 to 8 mmol/L. Step 1: EK = 61.5 x log(8/140), about -76 mV instead of -95 mV. Step 2: because IK1 dominates resting conductance, the resting potential moves up to about -70 mV. Step 3: at this potential many fast Na+ channels stay inactivated between beats. Step 4: phase 0 is slower and smaller, conduction slows, and the QRS widens. Step 5: high extracellular K+ increases IKr conductance, so phase 3 speeds up and T waves become peaked, usually before the QRS widens. Step 6: if most Na+ channels are inactivated, conduction fails and ventricular fibrillation or asystole can follow.

sections.title: Excitation-contraction coupling and calcium-induced calcium release

blocks.text: Excitation-contraction coupling converts the sarcolemmal action potential into sarcomere force, and in the heart the link is Ca2+. T tubules carry the action potential into the cell at the Z lines. Where a T tubule meets one SR terminal cisterna it forms a dyad, and across a cleft of about 12 to 15 nm, L-type Ca2+ channels face clusters of RyR2. Atrial myocytes have few T tubules, so their Ca2+ release spreads inward from the surface. Diastolic cytosolic free Ca2+ is about 0.1 µmol/L, roughly ten thousand times lower than extracellular ionized Ca2+ (about 1.1 to 1.3 mmol/L), and the SR holds a large store buffered by calsequestrin.

During the plateau, trigger Ca2+ entering the tiny cleft binds RyR2 and opens it. One cluster releasing Ca2+ produces a Ca2+ spark, and thousands of synchronized sparks form the Ca2+ transient, which raises cytosolic Ca2+ to about 1 µmol/L. In human ventricle the SR supplies most activator Ca2+, about 70 percent. Release is graded: each L-type channel controls only its facing cluster, so a larger trigger or a fuller SR releases more Ca2+. These two levers are what sympathetic stimulation, beat frequency, and changes in Na+ handling adjust (C03 to C05). Release ends within tens of milliseconds, mainly because falling local SR Ca2+ lowers RyR2 open probability.

Ca2+ binds the single regulatory site of cardiac troponin C (fast skeletal TnC has two), which then grips troponin I, which releases actin, and tropomyosin rolls deeper into the groove, uncovering myosin-binding sites. Myosin heads carrying ADP and Pi bind actin, release Pi in the power stroke, and release ADP into the rigor state; a new ATP must bind before the head detaches, and its hydrolysis recocks the head. Adult human ventricle expresses mainly the slower, economical beta myosin heavy chain.

blocks.text: Because cardiac coupling has no mechanical link, removing extracellular Ca2+ or blocking L-type channels weakens the heart promptly while sparing skeletal muscle. RyR2 must also stay closed in diastole. Leaky RyR2 or loss of calsequestrin causes catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia: under adrenergic stress, SR Ca2+ escapes in diastole, NCX extrudes it while bringing in 3 Na+ per Ca2+, and the net inward current produces delayed afterdepolarizations. Glycoside toxicity and failing myocardium share this mechanism.

blocks.predict: An isolated heart and an isolated skeletal muscle are both moved into a Ca2+-free solution. What happens to contraction in each over the next minute, and why?
blocks.explain: Cardiac contractions weaken rapidly and stop, because no trigger Ca2+ enters to open RyR2 and the SR store runs down through NCX. The skeletal muscle keeps twitching for a time, because its voltage sensor opens RyR1 mechanically.

sections.title: Relaxation and calcium removal; why ischemia impairs both phases

blocks.text: Relaxation is active. Cytosolic Ca2+ must fall from about 1 to 0.1 µmol/L so Ca2+ leaves troponin C, and each attached myosin head needs a fresh ATP to release actin. SERCA2a pumps 2 Ca2+ into the SR per ATP and removes about 70 percent of activator Ca2+; its speed largely sets early diastolic relaxation. Unphosphorylated phospholamban lowers SERCA2a Ca2+ affinity; phosphorylation by PKA or CaMKII releases this brake, so phosphorylation activates the pump. NCX removes most of the rest, exchanging 3 Na+ in for 1 Ca2+ out. It is electrogenic and depends on the Na+ gradient kept by the Na+/K+-ATPase, so it slows or reverses when cytosolic Na+ rises or the membrane stays depolarized.

blocks.title: Ca2+ cycling in one heartbeat
steps: L-type channels admit a small trigger Ca2+ influx
RyR2 releases most activator Ca2+ from the SR
Ca2+ binds troponin C and cross-bridges generate force
SERCA2a returns most Ca2+ to the SR
NCX exports an amount equal to what entered
Cytosolic Ca2+ returns to about 0.1 µmol/L and the muscle relaxes
blocks.caption: In a steady state, reuptake balances release and extrusion balances entry. Shifting either balance changes SR load and the strength of later beats.

blocks.text: Why ischemia impairs contraction and relaxation

The myocyte stores little energy and depends on aerobic metabolism. When coronary flow stops, creatine phosphate falls and anaerobic glycolysis produces lactate and H+. Force falls within about 60 s, while ATP is still substantial, because H+ lowers troponin C Ca2+ sensitivity and Pi reduces force per cross-bridge. Relaxation fails because SERCA2a and PMCA slow as ADP and Pi accumulate and ATP falls and NCX loses its driving force as Na+ rises (Na+/H+ exchange adds more Na+), so Ca2+ lingers and cross-bridges stay attached; severe depletion produces rigor and ischemic contracture. Impaired relaxation therefore appears first in the ischemic cascade, before reduced wall motion, ECG changes, and angina.

blocks.title: From ATP loss to stiff, weak myocardium
steps: Coronary occlusion halts oxidative phosphorylation
Glycolysis produces lactate and H+; Pi accumulates
Ca2+ sensitivity and force fall within about 60 s
Na+/K+-ATPase slows; Na+ rises and NCX fails
SERCA2a slows; diastolic Ca2+ stays high
Stiff ventricle raises end-diastolic pressure
Ca2+ overload causes irreversible injury after about 20 to 40 min
blocks.caption: The same energy failure weakens systole and impairs diastole. With reperfusion, Ca2+ overload causes hypercontraction and contraction band necrosis (CV-18-C).

blocks.title: Inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase
blocks.text: Digoxin partially inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase. Step 1: cytosolic Na+ rises a few mmol/L. Step 2: the smaller Na+ gradient slows NCX, so less Ca2+ leaves the cell each diastole. Step 3: SERCA2a pumps the retained Ca2+ into the SR. Step 4: over several beats SR content rises until extrusion again matches entry. Step 5: each beat releases more Ca2+, so contraction strengthens without any receptor signaling. Step 6: with excessive inhibition the SR overloads, releases Ca2+ spontaneously in diastole, and NCX turns that release into delayed afterdepolarizations. Ischemia, which also raises Na+, drives Ca2+ overload by the same route.

sections.title: Beta-1 adrenergic regulation of contraction and relaxation

blocks.text: Norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves and epinephrine from the adrenal medulla act on beta-1 receptors, the predominant beta receptors of ventricular myocytes. Within seconds, contraction becomes stronger, faster, and shorter, and relaxation speeds up. This matters because sympathetic activation also raises heart rate (CV-7), which shortens diastole more than systole, so the ventricle fills only if it relaxes faster.

The beta-1 receptor couples to Gs, which stimulates adenylyl cyclase (mainly types 5 and 6) to make cAMP. cAMP frees the catalytic subunits of protein kinase A, and A-kinase anchoring proteins hold PKA near its targets. Phosphodiesterases (mainly PDE3 and PDE4), phosphatases, and receptor desensitization by G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 and beta-arrestin end the signal.

Gs alpha stimulates adenylyl cyclase; cAMP rises
cAMP activates protein kinase A
PKA phosphorylates L-type channels, phospholamban, and troponin I
Larger Ca2+ transient: positive inotropy
Faster Ca2+ removal: positive lusitropy

blocks.title: Protein kinase A targets in the ventricular myocyte
rows: Greater open probability and longer openings
Larger trigger and SR release: stronger contraction
Faster reuptake (relaxation) and higher SR load (stronger beats)

blocks.caption: The first three targets are the core of the response: a shorter, stronger twitch that fits the shorter cycle of a fast heart rate.

blocks.text: Phospholamban phosphorylation serves both effects: within a beat Ca2+ falls faster, and over successive beats the SR captures more Ca2+ before NCX removes it, so release grows. Troponin I phosphorylation alone would slightly lower force at a given Ca2+, but the larger transient more than compensates. Enhanced IKs keeps repolarization in step with the larger plateau current, which is why exercise provokes arrhythmias in long QT type 1 (loss of IKs). RyR2 phosphorylation is also reported, but its importance is debated.

Beta-1 stimulation raises force at any sarcomere length, shifting the ventricular function curve upward (CV-6) rather than moving along it. Vagal effects on ventricular contractility are small because ventricular parasympathetic innervation is sparse. In chronic heart failure, sustained sympathetic drive downregulates beta-1 receptors, increases G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2, reduces SERCA2a, and leaves phospholamban underphosphorylated, giving weaker contraction, slower relaxation, a blunted exercise response, and more arrhythmias.

blocks.predict: A mouse expresses a mutant phospholamban that cannot be phosphorylated but still binds SERCA2a. How will its heart respond to a beta-1 agonist compared with a normal heart?
blocks.explain: Heart rate and L-type Ca2+ current still rise, so contractility increases somewhat. SERCA2a stays inhibited, so reuptake does not speed up, the SR store grows less, and relaxation accelerates far less (mainly the troponin I effect remains). Filling suffers at high rates.

sections.title: The cardiac length-tension relationship and how force is graded

blocks.text: Active force depends on how many myosin heads can reach actin. Thick filaments are about 1.6 µm and thin filaments about 1 µm long, so overlap is optimal at about 2.0 to 2.2 µm. On the descending limb, stretch reduces overlap until force reaches zero near 3.6 µm in classic skeletal muscle studies. On the ascending limb, thin filaments from opposite sides interfere with each other, and at very short lengths thick filaments butt against the Z lines.

Ventricular sarcomeres work on the ascending limb, from about 1.8 to 1.9 µm at low filling to about 2.2 µm at normal to high filling. Over this range force rises several times more than overlap alone predicts because of length-dependent activation: stretch makes the myofilaments more sensitive to Ca2+, shifting the force versus Ca2+ curve to the left, so the same Ca2+ transient produces more force. Proposed mechanisms include titin strain that positions more myosin heads to bind actin, narrower filament spacing as the cell thins, and cooperative Ca2+ binding to troponin C. A slower rise in the Ca2+ transient develops over minutes after sustained stretch, but the beat-to-beat Frank-Starling response comes from overlap and Ca2+ sensitivity (CV-6).

Stiff cardiac titin isoforms and collagen make passive tension rise steeply above about 2.2 µm, so intact hearts rarely reach the descending limb. A dilated failing heart weakens from reduced contractility, higher wall stress, and mitral regurgitation, not overstretch, because chronic volume overload adds sarcomeres in series. A stiff ventricle (hypertrophy, fibrosis, ischemia) needs higher filling pressure to reach the same volume.

Skeletal muscle grades force by recruiting motor units (size principle) and by summating twitches at higher firing rates. The heart can do neither, because every myocyte contracts each beat and the refractory period prevents summation (C01). It grades force within each cell through Ca2+ delivery (raised by beta-1 stimulation and by higher rate, which loads the SR in the positive force-frequency relationship, blunted in failing hearts), myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity (raised by stretch, lowered by acidosis and troponin I phosphorylation), and sarcomere length. These levers work because a normal Ca2+ transient does not saturate troponin C. A preload effect moves the heart along its curve with little change in the Ca2+ transient; an inotropic effect enlarges the transient and shifts the curve upward.

blocks.predict: A cardiac muscle strip is stretched from 1.9 to 2.2 µm and its active force roughly doubles, yet filament overlap has changed only modestly. What accounts for the rest, and would a skeletal fiber show as large a change?
blocks.explain: Most of the increase reflects length-dependent activation: the myofilaments become more sensitive to Ca2+, so the same transient recruits more cross-bridges. A skeletal fiber near its optimum relies on overlap alone and changes much less.

integration.text: Structure sets up every mechanism here. Intercalated discs combine force-transmitting junctions with gap junctions, so the ventricle conducts and contracts as one unit and cannot recruit cells. Dyads at the Z lines place L-type channels against RyR2, and the myocyte's dense mitochondria reflect its dependence on coronary O2. Biochemistry ties it together: myosin ATPase, SERCA2a, PMCA, and the Na+/K+-ATPase all need ATP, and Gs, cAMP, and PKA link the autonomic nervous system to the Ca2+ transient.

Pathology follows the same logic. Sarcomere gene mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3) cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; KCNQ1, KCNH2, and SCN5A mutations cause long QT syndromes; RYR2 or calsequestrin mutations cause catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; skeletal RYR1 mutations cause malignant hyperthermia, a primary disorder of skeletal muscle. For any question, name the cellular lever first (trigger Ca2+, SR load, Ca2+ removal, myofilament sensitivity, or sarcomere length), then reason outward to the organ.

summary: Ventricular myocytes rest at about -90 mV because IK1 dominates resting conductance and holds the membrane near EK.
Phase 0 is fast Na+ influx, phase 1 is Na+ inactivation with Ito, phase 2 is L-type Ca2+ influx balanced by K+ efflux, and phase 3 is delayed rectifier K+ efflux followed by IK1.
The effective refractory period (about 0.25 to 0.3 s) lasts nearly as long as contraction, preventing summation and tetany.
Raised extracellular K+ depolarizes the resting membrane, inactivates Na+ channels, slows conduction, and speeds repolarization.
Trigger Ca2+ through T-tubule L-type channels opens RyR2 in the dyad, so cardiac contraction requires extracellular Ca2+; skeletal Cav1.1 opens RyR1 mechanically.
SERCA2a removes about 70 percent of activator Ca2+ into the SR and NCX (3 Na+ in per Ca2+ out) most of the rest; phospholamban phosphorylation relieves SERCA2a inhibition.
Ischemia impairs relaxation first (SERCA2a, PMCA, and NCX failure) and contraction soon after (acidosis, Pi, and reduced SR loading).
Beta-1 signaling through Gs, cAMP, and PKA phosphorylates L-type channels, phospholamban, and troponin I, producing a stronger, faster, shorter twitch.
Cardiac sarcomeres work on the ascending limb (about 1.8 to 2.2 µm), where stretch raises both overlap and myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity; stiff titin and collagen keep them off the descending limb.
Skeletal muscle grades force by recruitment and summation; cardiac muscle grades it by Ca2+ delivery, Ca2+ sensitivity, and sarcomere length.

verify: The fractions of Ca2+ removed by SERCA2a (about 70 percent), NCX (about 25 to 30 percent), and the slow systems (about 1 to 2 percent) come mainly from rabbit ventricular myocytes, which are taken to resemble human ventricle; confirm whether NABNE expects specific percentages.
The SR share of activator Ca2+ in human ventricle (about 70 percent) is an approximate consensus figure that varies between species and sources.

Ventricular action potential duration and refractory period values (about 0.25 to 0.3 s, relative refractory period about 0.05 s) follow Guyton and Hall; other sources quote slightly different figures.
Ventricular threshold (about -70 mV) and overshoot (about +20 mV) vary between sources by several millivolts.
Sarcomere working range (about 1.8 to 2.2 µm), filament lengths, and the 3.6 µm zero-overlap length are approximate and partly derived from frog skeletal muscle studies.
The relative contributions of titin strain, lattice spacing, and troponin C cooperativity to length-dependent activation are still debated; this chapter presents them as proposed mechanisms.
The functional importance of PKA phosphorylation of RyR2, and the role of RyR2 leak in human heart failure, are debated in the literature.
Timing of ischemic injury (loss of contractility within about 60 s, irreversible injury after about 20 to 40 min) follows Robbins; confirm the values NABNE expects.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects channel gene names (SCN5A, KCNH2, KCNQ1, RYR2) and current names (IK1, Ito, IKr, IKs) or only descriptive terms.
